RxJS Stream Control

RxJS Stream Control is the recommended mechanism for debouncing, switching, cancellation, and other temporal or concurrency-driven stream behaviors before values enter the pipeline. is a state orchestration framework—it consumes values deterministically, but it does not shape the streams that produce them.

This document explains the boundary between RxJS stream shaping and state orchestration, and demonstrates the canonical pattern: apply RxJS operators upstream, then pass the resulting Observable<T> into fromStream().

Key Principle

should never compete with RxJS. It should cooperate with it. does not care how values arrive — only that they arrive — and that state transitions remain deterministic once they do.

Why Opts to Delegate Pre-Pipeline Stream Control to RxJS

is not responsible for time-based stream shaping, event suppression, scheduling heuristics, or concurrency strategies for async sources.

Stream concerns such as the following are handled upstream using RxJS:

  • Debounce, audit, sampling, and buffering
  • Cancellation and switching (switchMap, exhaustMap, concatMap)
  • Backpressure strategies
  • Retry and timing heuristics at the stream level
  • Deduplication and distinctness

These problems are already solved by RxJS using well-tested, composable, declarative operators. Re-implementing them inside would duplicate abstractions, expand the API surface, and blur the boundary between temporal policy and state orchestration.

Policy Controllers vs RxJS

The Policy Layer and RxJS solve different classes of problems, and both are intentionally supported by .

RxJS is the preferred tool for pre-pipeline stream shaping: debouncing, buffering, cancellation, concurrency control, and temporal composition before values are submitted to the pipeline.

Policy Controllers exist for cases where execution decisions must be made inside the pipeline lifecycle—based on attempt identity, failure state, re-entry rules, or interaction with other pipeline stages.

Use RxJS when:

  • Timing and suppression occur before pipeline admission
  • Events may be safely dropped, merged, or canceled upstream
  • No awareness of pipeline attempts, retries, or failures is required
  • Stream semantics are sufficient to express the desired behavior

Use Policy Controllers when:

  • Execution decisions depend on pipeline attempts rather than raw events
  • Failures must trigger retries, revotes, or aborts
  • Execution must pause and later re-enter the pipeline
  • Decisions must interact with pipeline stages or global Vault state
  • Suppressed work must be reconsidered rather than discarded

In short, RxJS controls whether a value exists. Once an execution is admitted, Policy Controllers ensure it resolves deterministically—even under failure or re-entry.

Design Boundary

If a concern can be expressed entirely through stream composition, it belongs in RxJS. If a concern requires awareness of pipeline lifecycle, failures, or re-entry semantics, it belongs in the Policy Layer.

Pre-Pipeline Delegation with RxJS

intentionally delegates pre-pipeline stream shaping to RxJS. Temporal control, suppression, buffering, cancellation, and concurrency are applied before values are admitted into the pipeline.

Whether a value represents a continuous stream or a single state candidate, assumes that any value it receives has already been shaped intentionally. Once a value enters the pipeline, treats it as authoritative and eligible for deterministic state orchestration.

Continuous Streams: fromStream()

fromStream() is the canonical integration seam for continuous or multi-emission sources. It accepts an Observable<T> and establishes a subscription that forwards each emitted value into the pipeline as a distinct state update.

RxJS operators are composed upstream. does not participates in stream suppression or scheduling.

RxJS fromStream State

{{`this.vault.fromStream(
  events$.pipe(
    debounceTime(300),
    distinctUntilChanged();`}}
 
{{`employeeCell.fromStream(
  events$.pipe(
    debounceTime(300),
    distinctUntilChanged();`}}

Single Candidates: replaceState() and mergeState()

RxJS is equally appropriate for single-candidate state updates. When an observable is supplied to replaceState() or mergeState(), resolves exactly one emitted value and forwards it through the pipeline.

This pattern is ideal for deferred, conditional, or asynchronously composed state candidates without converting them into continuous streams.

RxJS Replace State

{{`this.vault.replaceState(
  fetchEmployee$.pipe(
    timeout(2000)
  )
);`}}
 
{{`employeeCell.replaceState(
  fetchEmployee$.pipe(
    timeout(2000)
  )
);`}}

RxJS Merge State

{{`this.vault.mergeState(
  update$.pipe(
    map(partial => ({ status: 'ready', ...partial }))
  )
);`}}
 
{{`employeeCell.mergeState(
  update$.pipe(
    map(partial => ({ status: 'ready', ...partial }))
  )
);`}}

Design Rule

Stream suppression, timing, and cancellation belong before pipeline admission. If a value enters , assumes you intended it to. RxJS defines when values exist; defines how those values are orchestrated into state.

Common RxJS Recipes

The examples below show common RxJS patterns used to achieve debounce, throttling, buffering, switching, and deduplication before receives values.

Debounce User Input

Use debounceTime to delay emission until input stabilizes: 

{{`import { debounceTime, map } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(
  inputChange$.pipe(
    map(e => e.target.value),
    debounceTime(300)
  )
);`}}
 
{{`import { debounceTime, map } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(
  inputChange$.pipe(
    map(e => e.target.value),
    debounceTime(300)
  )
);`}}

Throttle Burst Events

Use throttleTime to allow at most one emission per window: 

{{`import { throttleTime } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(
  scroll$.pipe(
    throttleTime(250)
  )
);`}}
 
{{`import { throttleTime } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(
  scroll$.pipe(
    throttleTime(250)
  )
);`}}

Audit or Sample at a Fixed Cadence

Use auditTime or sampleTime to control cadence without suppressing upstream events: 

{{`import { auditTime, sampleTime } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(events$.pipe(auditTime(1000)));
this.vault.fromStream(events$.pipe(sampleTime(1000)));`}}
 
{{`import { auditTime, sampleTime } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(events$.pipe(auditTime(1000)));
employeeCell.fromStream(events$.pipe(sampleTime(1000)));`}}

Distinct Until Changed

Prevent redundant updates when the value has not meaningfully changed: 

{{`import { distinctUntilChanged } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(
  value$.pipe(
    distinctUntilChanged()
  )
);`}}
 
{{`import { distinctUntilChanged } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(
  value$.pipe(
    distinctUntilChanged()
  )
);`}}

Buffer Events Over Time

Batch events into arrays using bufferTime:

{{`import { bufferTime, filter } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(
  actions$.pipe(
    bufferTime(500),
    filter(batch => batch.length > 0)
  )
);`}}
 
{{`import { bufferTime, filter } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(
  actions$.pipe(
    bufferTime(500),
    filter(batch => batch.length > 0)
  )
);`}}

Switch to the Latest Async Request

Use switchMap when only the latest request should remain active. Prior requests are cancelled at the stream level. 

{{`import { switchMap } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(
  query$.pipe(
    switchMap(q => fetchEmployees$(q))
  )
);`}}
 
{{`import { switchMap } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(
  query$.pipe(
    switchMap(q => fetchEmployees$(q))
  )
);`}}

Ignore New Requests While Busy

Use exhaustMap to ignore new triggers while an async task is running (useful for submit buttons). 

{{`import { exhaustMap } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(
  submitClicks$.pipe(
    exhaustMap(() => submitForm$())
  )
);`}}
 
{{`import { exhaustMap } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(
  submitClicks$.pipe(
    exhaustMap(() => submitForm$())
  )
);`}}

Queue Requests Sequentially

Use concatMap to guarantee ordering by running async work sequentially, one at a time. 

{{`import { concatMap } from 'rxjs/operators';

this.vault.fromStream(
  requests$.pipe(
    concatMap(req => processRequest$(req))
  )
);`}}
 
{{`import { concatMap } from 'rxjs/operators';

employeeCell.fromStream(
  requests$.pipe(
    concatMap(req => processRequest$(req))
  )
);`}}
Separation of Concerns

stays small and deterministic by keeping stream shaping separate from state orchestration. The table below summarizes where each responsibility belongs.

Responsibility Boundaries
Layer Responsibility
RxJS Time, scheduling, buffering, cancellation, switching, concurrency, and stream composition
Pipeline Deterministic state orchestration, lifecycle boundaries, resolution, merge, reduction, and snapshots
Policy Layer Execution policy, retries, revotes, aborts, permissions, and centralized arbitration
UI User interaction, rendering, and presentation-level coordination

Rule of Thumb

If the problem is about time or concurrency, solve it in RxJS. If the problem is about execution authority or permission to proceed, solve it in the Policy Layer. If the problem is about authoritative state, solve it in .

Guidance and Pitfalls

Do: Shape Streams Upstream

  • Use RxJS operators to debounce, throttle, batch, or cancel before calling fromStream().
  • Keep updates semantically meaningful: emit values you actually want orchestrated.

Do: Prefer Explicitness Over Magic

  • Stream behavior should be visible in the stream definition (pipe(...)), not hidden in .
  • Temporal rules should remain readable and testable without the pipeline present.

Avoid: Recreating RxJS Inside

  • Do not add time-based or cancellation heuristics inside behaviors purely for stream control.
  • Do not rely on “hidden timing” inside the pipeline to compensate for missing stream composition upstream.
Note

RxJS controls what enters the pipeline and when it enters. Once a value enters , the pipeline proceeds deterministically under the rules of orchestration and policy.
